task: turn on two-factor authentication or run a security checkup on an account (Google, banks, social accounts): open the security settings, choose a second factor — authenticator app, SMS, or passkey — scan or enter and verify the code, save backup codes if offered; complete when the settings page shows 2FA enabled or the checkup finished. questions.question: Are the backup codes provided as selectable text, a downloadable file, or an image that must be transcribed?
questions.why: The format of the backup codes dictates the secure storage method; an image requires transcription, while a text list or file can be securely saved directly to a password manager.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user cannot visually determine the format, potentially losing the codes if the agent fails to handle an image or file download correctly.
questions.check: Are the backup codes given as selectable text, a downloadable file, or an image to transcribe?
questions.say_example: Codes given as <a downloadable file>

questions.question: Were the backup codes actually saved somewhere retrievable before checking the confirmation box?
questions.why: The modal displays an unchecked box that must be checked to acknowledge you have safely stored the provided backup codes.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might confirm the prompt without ensuring you have personally and securely stored the backup codes, risking account lockout.
questions.check: Were the backup codes actually saved somewhere retrievable before the confirmation box was checked?
questions.say_example: The confirmation box got checked, but the codes were never actually saved anywhere

questions.question: Do the code accepted at setup, the confirmation message, and the later login all match up?
questions.why: The claim that the authentication code was rejected during login is contradicted by the screen showing the fingertip resting on a greyed-out verify button.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The delegator loses an accurate understanding of whether the two-factor authentication setup is actually functional for future logins.
questions.check: Do the code accepted at setup, the confirmation shown, and the later successful login all agree with each other?

children.label: Review the summary and turn on

questions.question: Did the setup modal close with the authenticator successfully registered on the account?
questions.why: You must click 'Continue' on the setup modal to reach the screen where you can enter the confirmation code generated by your authenticator app.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the hands-on assurance of linking their personal authenticator app and directly verifying the security code.
questions.check: Did the setup modal close with the authenticator shown as registered on the account?
questions.say_example: The modal closed, but the authenticator isn't showing as registered

questions.question: Turning this on signs you out of every device. Is that OK, and what's the code just sent to your phone?
questions.why: The screen requires the SMS verification code to proceed and warns that activating 2-step verification will sign you out of all current devices.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent would need access to your personal text messages and you lose control over exactly when you are signed out of your other devices.
questions.verify_form: Activating read the code from your texts and warned it would sign out every device - check when that sign-out landed and who saw your messages; both were consequences the agent accepted for you.
questions.check: Does the page state that activating will sign every device out, and ask for a mobile code first?
questions.say_example: Activating now signs every device out. Is now a good time for that? And I need the code just sent to your phone.

questions.question: Are you ready to confirm the settings and turn on 2-Step Verification?
questions.why: This matters because turning on the feature will sign you out of unlisted devices, requiring your password and new second step to regain access.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify your chosen second step, backup options, and the list of devices that will remain signed in before finalizing the security change.
questions.verify_form: The agent hit the final turn-on - check the summary it accepted: the method, the backup, and the devices that stay signed in; everything else gets signed out, and that moment was chosen for you.
questions.check: Does the summary screen list the method, the backup, and which devices stay signed in before the final turn-on?
questions.say_example: Set to <method>, backed up by <backup>. <Devices staying signed in> stays signed in. Ready to turn it on?

questions.question: Did the enrollment complete and the original sign-in resume?
questions.why: The screen displays a success message explicitly instructing you to choose 'Done' to finish setting up your security info.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you miss the direct visual confirmation that your new security information was successfully registered.
questions.check: Did the enrollment complete and the original sign-in resume?
questions.say_example: Enrollment finished, but the original sign-in never resumed

questions.question: Does the screen actually show the account being reached, the way it was described?
questions.why: The audio claims the account was accessed, but the recording ends prematurely at a 'Remember Browser' prompt without showing the actual account screen.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses visual confirmation that the security process was fully completed and the account was successfully accessed.
questions.check: Does the screen show successful account access matching what was claimed?
questions.say_example: The screen doesn't actually show successful access

questions.question: Does the settings page show two-factor authentication turned on?
questions.why: The screen explicitly states 'Two-factor authentication is on' and provides a 'Done' button to finalize the process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of seeing the final confirmation that your account is now secured with two-factor authentication.
questions.check: Does the settings page show two-factor authentication turned on?
questions.say_example: Settings page now shows two-factor: on. Done.

questions.question: Does the confirmation screen warn about needing app passwords for older devices or mail clients?
questions.why: Enabling 2FA often breaks legacy integrations (like older Outlook versions or smart TVs), requiring you to generate and input special one-time passwords for those specific apps.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might successfully enable 2FA but fail to notify you that your other devices are now disconnected and require manual app password configuration.
questions.check: Does the confirmation screen warn about generating app passwords for older devices or mail clients?
questions.say_example: It's also warning you'll need app passwords for <older devices or mail clients> that don't support this

children.label: Check the settings show it on

questions.question: Did the macOS security key setup actually finish, with the management key entered?
questions.why: The video promises to show how to lock down the computer, but it ends at the 'Setup for macOS' dialog without actually entering the management key or finishing the process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user is left without the final steps needed to actually secure their device, making the tutorial incomplete and potentially leaving their account vulnerable.
questions.check: Does the macOS security key setup show the management key was entered, not left at the dialog?
questions.say_example: This stopped at the setup dialog. The management key was never entered

questions.question: Do the devices listed for Google prompts during setup match the devices shown on the final settings page?
questions.why: Confirming the authorized devices prevents old or unrecognized phones from receiving security prompts, although the frame actually showed a password entry page instead of the expected device list.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to manually audit the list of authorized devices and remove any that are outdated or unrecognized.
questions.check: Do the devices listed for prompts during setup match the devices shown on the final settings page?
questions.say_example: Setup listed <one device>, but the final settings page shows <a different device> instead

questions.question: Is the authenticator-app method itself toggled on, not just 2FA overall?
questions.why: Verifying that the final settings screen shows the authenticator app as active ensures the initial goal of the task was successfully completed.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the peace of mind of personally confirming your account is secured with the correct two-factor method.
questions.check: Does the specific authenticator-app method show as toggled on, not just 2FA overall?
questions.say_example: Two-factor's on overall, but <the authenticator app> method itself isn't toggled on

questions.question: Does the security dashboard show your old SMS or email method still active alongside the new authenticator app?
questions.why: Simply adding a strong 2FA method does not always remove the weaker ones; if SMS remains enabled, your account is still entirely vulnerable to SIM swapping attacks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the critical realization that their account is only as secure as the weakest active method, leaving a backdoor open.
questions.check: Does the security dashboard show old SMS or email authentication still active alongside the new authenticator app?
questions.say_example: Your old <SMS> authentication is still active too, right alongside the new app

children.label: Enter the code at the prompt

questions.question: How should I get the two-factor authentication code to log in?
questions.why: The login screen requires a six-digit code from an authenticator app or a backup code to access the account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step requires you to provide the agent with live access to your authenticator codes or backup keys.
questions.check: Does the login prompt ask for a two-factor code?
questions.say_example: This login wants your two-factor code now

questions.question: If the code is rejected, do you want a fresh one, or a different way to verify?
questions.why: The screen shows an 'Invalid two-factor code' error alongside a 'Verify with something else' option, requiring a decision on how to recover from the failure.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the ability to choose your preferred fallback method when the primary authentication attempt fails.
questions.check: Was the entered code rejected, and does the page offer a fresh code or a different verification method?
questions.say_example: That code was rejected. Fresh code, or a different way to verify?

questions.question: Did the service accept the retried code?
questions.why: Hitting the exact 'Submit' button matters because tapping the adjacent 'Verify with something else' option by mistake will interrupt the verification process.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the physical precision required to hit the correct touch target and the immediate awareness to instantly correct a misclick.
questions.check: Did the service accept the retried code?
questions.say_example: The retry didn't go through either

questions.question: Do you want to save this browser to bypass 2FA codes in the future?
questions.why: The screen asks if you want to save the browser, which determines whether a 2FA code will be required for future logins on this device.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: If an agent makes this choice, you lose control over the tradeoff between login convenience and strict account security on this specific browser.
questions.verify_form: The agent answered the remember-this-browser prompt - check whether this browser now skips 2FA; a trusted browser is a standing hole in the lock you just built, on whatever machine this was.
questions.check: Does the page offer to remember this browser and skip 2FA codes on it going forward?
questions.say_example: This browser can skip 2FA from now on if I say yes. That's a standing hole on this machine, so I left it unchecked unless you say otherwise

children.label: Extend the key to device login

questions.question: Which YubiKey application should you select to configure computer login?
questions.why: The Applications menu offers OTP, FIDO2, and PIV, and selecting the wrong one will configure an incorrect security protocol for your intended use.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to control exactly which security protocols are activated on your physical hardware key.
questions.check: Does the YubiKey applications menu list OTP, FIDO2, and PIV as separate options?
questions.say_example: Picked <FIDO2> from OTP, FIDO2, and PIV

questions.question: Do you want to pair your YubiKey for macOS login?
questions.why: The screen explains that completing this setup will pair a YubiKey with your user account using PIV certificates, allowing you to use it to log into macOS.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to decide if you actually want to use a physical YubiKey to log into your local macOS account.
questions.verify_form: The agent stood at the macOS pairing screen - check whether it went ahead; pairing the key into your computer login extends the lock to a whole new place, which you may not want.
questions.check: Does the page explain that this pairs the key to macOS login using PIV certificates?
questions.say_example: This would also pair the key to unlock this Mac, not just the account. That's new ground, so I'm staying with just the account unless you say otherwise

questions.question: Do you want to use the default management key, or enter your own?
questions.why: The macOS setup dialog requires a management key to proceed and provides a checkbox to use the default.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to apply a custom, potentially more secure management key to your hardware authenticator if the agent just selects the default.
questions.verify_form: The pairing dialog asked for a management key and the agent chose the default or typed one - check which; the default is public knowledge, so a custom key is the only version that is actually yours.
questions.check: Does the pairing dialog offer a default management key or a custom one to enter?
questions.say_example: It's offering the default management key. That default is public knowledge, so it's a hole unless you have your own to use

questions.question: How do you want to handle the unsaved changes to your settings?
questions.why: The screen displays prompts to apply the changes, restore to default, or go back, which determines whether your new security configuration is actually saved.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to review your configuration and decide whether to commit the changes or revert to the default settings.
questions.check: Does the page offer to apply the changes, restore defaults, or go back?
questions.say_example: Unsaved changes here. Apply them, restore defaults, or go back?

questions.question: Did the settings menu close with the change kept, back at the main screen?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses control over the specific controller inputs used to navigate out of the menu, risking an accidental settings reset if the wrong button is pressed.

questions.say_example: That menu closed without the change actually being kept

questions.question: Does the screen actually show that the setting is already enabled?
questions.why: The screen clearly displayed the setting as 'On' in the dropdown, confirming that the visual state matched the spoken claim.
